description: I'm Fernando Góes from Brazil, developer of OPHIDIAN VI — a pulsed inductive electric thruster for LEO → LLO cargo missions — and OHM, the AI that supervises it. I bring propulsion, mission design, and interactive simulation. Join us to build a Space Mission Design Game where players design a real mission and face real engineering trade-offs. Looking for 1 developer / NASA data and 1 designer / video storyteller.
summary:
We developed MISSION ARCHITECT, a playable space mission design game for the Space Mission Design Game challenge.

Players design a complete mission — destination, crew, spacecraft, propulsion, life support, spares, and shielding — then manage it in flight and face the consequences in a debrief. The game models real constraints using public NASA references: oxygen consumption, CO2 buildup, water recycling, food, power, mass, Delta-V from the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, ECLSS limits, Orion 21-day consumables for four crew, and radiation dose.

OPHIDIAN VI appears as one of four propulsion options, not as the whole game. Chemical, electric, nuclear thermal, and OPHIDIAN VI each force different trade-offs in mass, time, and risk.

It matters because most mission failures will not come from lack of thrust, but from logistics: one missing filter, one kilogram too much, one day without water. MISSION ARCHITECT teaches that spaceflight is designed, not just flown.
details:
This project was built for the official 2026 challenge: Space Mission Design Game. It answers the challenge by turning mission design into a playable system: the player designs a complete mission, manages life support and logistics in flight, and learns from a debrief — not just by choosing a rocket, but by keeping a crew alive.

MISSION ARCHITECT is a playable space mission design game. Players design a complete mission — destination (LEO, Moon, or Mars), crew size, spacecraft (Capsule, Habitat, or Cargo + Habitat), propulsion, life support, and spares — then manage it day by day in flight and face the consequences in a debrief.

The game runs on a closed-loop model with 8 live systems: Oxygen, CO2, Water, Food, Power, Mass, Spares / ORUs, and Radiation. Each day, the crew consumes resources using public NASA baselines: 0.84 kg of O2, 1.00 kg of CO2 exhaled, 2.28 kg of water, and 0.62 kg of food per person per day. Players choose one action per day — repair / recycle ECLSS, ration food and water, use a spare ORU, or add shielding — while random events occur: CO2 scrubber failure, water pump leak, solar particle event, power loss, and ORU failure. Delta-V is calculated from the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation. Orion's limit of 4 crew for up to 21 days and NASA's 600 mSv career radiation limit are built into the rules.

What benefits does it have?
It teaches systems thinking: spaceflight is not only thrust, it is logistics. A player learns why recycling, spares, and shielding matter more than a bigger engine on a long mission, and why one kilogram or one missing filter can decide survival.

What is the intended impact?
To make mission design accessible to students, players, and future engineers, and to show how real NASA constraints shape real missions to the Moon and Mars. The game can be used in classrooms, hackathons, and science outreach without installation or login.

What tools, languages, hardware, or software did you use?
Developed with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript as a single-file web game, hosted on GitHub Pages. No backend, no database, no login required. Game art was generated for this project. All physics and life-support numbers come from public NASA references.

How is it creative?
Most space games focus on piloting or building rockets. MISSION ARCHITECT focuses on the part nobody sees: ECLSS, consumables, ORUs, and radiation. OPHIDIAN VI appears as one of four propulsion options — Chemical, Electric, Nuclear Thermal, and OPHIDIAN VI — so the player must compare propulsion against life support, not choose a hero engine.

What factors did your team consider?
Mass, time, crew size, mission duration, recycling efficiency, spare parts, radiation dose, power, failure probability, and playability. Long missions were balanced to be possible only with recycling, spares, and shielding — just like real missions.
